newsitem.title: UK: Glaxo starts 200 mln stg inhaler programme.
newsitem.headline: Glaxo starts 200 mln stg inhaler programme.

text.p: Glaxo Wellcome Plc launched a 200 million stg programme targeted at the world's asthma sufferers on Thursday, but the British-based drugs giant is hoping that patients won't even notice. Glaxo, which controls more than a quarter of global respiratory drug sales, is embarking on the gradual conversion of gas-propelled asthma canisters from controversial CFCs to more ozone-friendly HFAs.
With around 16 different drug formulations and 160 million cans sold ever year in 80 different countries, Glaxo said the change-over is likely to take several years to complete.
"It's been quite a significant technical challenge," the group's respiratory diseases director Darrell Baker told Reuters. "Apart from the labels there isn't much we haven't had to change."

Baker said the switch to HFA gases, which resulted from the 1987 Montreal Protocol on reducing greenhouse gases, had involved 350 scientists in 12 research centres. Their task has been to ensure that the new puffers are as similar as possible to the old, with drugs reacting with the new gas to deliver exactly the same effect and dose.

Baker said the aim had been to create a "seamless transition, so that patients can use them in the same way as the old. Compliance does rely a lot on people's confidence in their inhalers. People need to be reassured that this will have the same effect on their asthma." Germany, where environmental concerns are particularly strong, is the first market to receive the new inhalers. "It tends to be the greener countries which are approving more quickly," said Baker. Denmark has also issued its first approval, while France and New Zealand have recommended authorisation. Glaxo Wellcome estimates that even in individual markets, the switch to HFA inhalers could take up to a year as doctors and patients are brought up to speed.

The company said it had spent 150 million stg on the switch, plus another 50 million stg on new manufacturing equipment. Its main inhaled asthma products are the veterans Ventolin and Becotide, together with the new drugs on the block, long-acting bronchodilator Serevent and inhaled steroid Flixotide. The company sold 1.76 billion stg of respiratory drugs last year, and the category overtook gastro-intestinal drugs as its most important product category in sales terms a few weeks ago.
